title: Locke

cards.b:
John Locke (1632–1704) is seen as the founder of liberalism. His ideas on consent, natural rights and the right to resist shaped the American Declaration of Independence (1776).

His main political work is the Two Treatises of Government, published in 1689 (dated 1690), soon after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 removed King James II.

The First Treatise attacks Robert Filmer's Patriarcha, which said kings inherit their power from Adam. The Second Treatise gives Locke's own theory. UPSC asks most about it.

Unlike Hobbes, Locke's state of nature is not a war of all against all. It is a state of liberty, not licence.

It is governed by the law of nature, which is reason. It teaches that since all are equal and independent, no one ought to harm another in their life, health, liberty or possessions.

So people have rights before any government exists. The state does not create these rights. It is set up only to protect them.

If the state of nature is peaceful, why leave it? Because it has three "inconveniences":

  • No settled, known law that all accept.
  • No impartial judge. Everyone judges their own case, and people are biased.
  • No power to enforce a just decision.

These can turn the state of nature into a state of war. So people form a civil society to fix them.

Chapter 5 of the Second Treatise gives the labour theory of property. God gave the earth to all in common. But each person owns their own body, and so their own labour.

When you mix your labour with something, such as picking acorns or ploughing land, it becomes yours.

Locke adds limits, called provisos: leave "enough and as good" for others, and do not take so much that it spoils. The invention of money, which does not spoil, lets people gather wealth without breaking the spoilage limit.

First, people agree to form a community and accept majority rule. Then the community sets up a government as a trustee. Unlike Hobbes's sovereign, Locke's government is bound by the terms of that trust.

• Consent: no one can be put under another's power without their consent. Locke allows tacit consent, such as using the roads or owning land.
  • Legislative supremacy: the legislature is the supreme power, but it is held in trust and cannot act arbitrarily.
  • Separation of powers: Locke separates legislative, executive and federative (foreign affairs) powers. Montesquieu later developed this further.
  • No taxation without consent of the people or their representatives.

If the government breaks its trust, for example by taking property without consent or ruling by force, it puts itself in a state of war with the people. The people may then resist and set up a new government. Locke says the people shall be judge.

In A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689), Locke argued the state should not force belief, because faith cannot be compelled. But his toleration had limits: he excluded atheists, and Catholics whom he saw as loyal to a foreign power.

• C.B. Macpherson argued Locke justified unlimited capitalist accumulation. Money removes the spoilage limit, and the propertyless are only partly members of society.
  • Carole Pateman, in The Sexual Contract (1988), said social contract theory hides a prior contract that subordinates women.
  • Post-colonial scholars note Locke helped run English colonies in Carolina and invested in the slave-trading Royal African Company. His idea of "waste" land was used to take Native American land.
  • Tacit consent is so wide that it means almost nothing.

The idea that government rests on consent appears in the Preamble: "We, the people of India" give ourselves the Constitution.

Natural rights thinking shapes Part III. In Puttaswamy (2017), the Supreme Court held privacy to be a fundamental right and said such rights are inherent, not gifts of the state.

Property is the twist. India removed the fundamental right to property by the 44th Amendment (1978). It is now only a constitutional right under Article 300A.

"Locke is the father of liberalism." Comment.
"Discuss Locke's theory of property and Macpherson's critique."
"Compare Hobbes's and Locke's social contracts."

Structure: peaceful state of nature, three inconveniences, property through labour, two-step contract and trust, limited government, the right to resist. End with critiques and India's Article 300A twist.

quiz.q: Locke's First Treatise attacked the ideas of…
quiz.w: It attacked Filmer's Patriarcha and the divine right of kings.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the inconveniences of Locke's state of nature?
quiz.w: Natural rights exist in Locke's state of nature. What is missing is law, judge and enforcement.

quiz.q: The power Locke calls 'federative' deals with…
quiz.w: The federative power manages relations with other communities.

o: Leave enough and as good for others
quiz.w: Enough and as good for others, and no spoilage.

quiz.q: In India, the right to property is now in…
quiz.w: The 44th Amendment (1978) moved it to Article 300A as a constitutional right.

sources: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689), Second Treatise chs. 2, 5, 7–9, 19
John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689)
C.B. Macpherson, The Political Theory of Possessive Individualism (1962)
Constitution of India, Art. 300A; Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
PYQ themes: Locke as liberal, property, consent and resistance (Paper I, repeated)
